LUNALOG — Smart Supply & Habitat Safety Node for Lunar and Mars Missions

Tagline: “Protecting supplies before they become a mission problem.”

Project Overview & The Problem
Moon and Mars exploration missions depend entirely on the survivability and integrity of transported supplies, including perishable food, sensitive pharmaceuticals, biological research samples, and mission-critical avionics. In the harsh extraterrestrial environment, cargo faces severe hazards such as extreme diurnal temperature swings from -130°C to +120°C, structural damage from rough regolith rover transport shocks exceeding 5G, and undetected container leaks or volatile chemical outgassing. Traditional space storage containers lack real-time localized diagnostics, creating a blind spot where cargo can quietly spoil or release toxic vapours inside habitats without the crew knowing until it is too late.

The Solution & Edge Hardware Architecture
LunaLog solves this challenge as an intelligent, low-cost IoT safety node attached directly to supply crates, rover bays, and habitat storage racks. Built around a high-performance ESP32 microcontroller, LunaLog incorporates multi-sensor fusion combining high-precision temperature probes, tri-axial vibration accelerometers, and gas/vapour sensors with dynamic temperature-and-humidity drift compensation algorithms. Operating with an offline-first architecture, the node continuously logs telemetry to local flash memory during communication blackouts, provides immediate physical alerts via onboard status LEDs, an OLED screen, and an audible warning buzzer, and automatically syncs data over Wi-Fi and WebSockets when connectivity is restored.

NASA Open Data Integration & Scientific Grounding
LunaLog deeply integrates public, verified NASA Open Data to contextualize onboard sensor telemetry with planetary science models. It incorporates the NASA CCMC DONKI API to monitor real-time space weather—including solar flares, coronal mass ejections, and solar energetic proton events—automatically applying an external risk factor (+10 points) to cargo exposed on the lunar surface. It utilizes the NASA POWER API to model diurnal ambient thermal curves across planetary analog sites like HI-SEAS Hawaii and Devon Island, and leverages NASA Solar System Treks (Moon LROC WAC and Mars Viking mosaics) along with NASA GIBS satellite imagery to deliver high-resolution cartographic base layers for global logistics tracking.

Autonomous Risk Engine & Crew Mission Dashboard
At the core of LunaLog is a real-time risk engine that converts complex raw telemetry into a transparent, actionable 0–100 safety score categorized into SAFE, WARNING, and CRITICAL thresholds. The node communicates seamlessly with an interactive Mission Control dashboard featuring live telemetry streams, dynamic risk breakdowns, 2D habitat layout mapping, and an autonomous AI self-healing engine capable of triggering simulated active cooling, airlock venting, or rover route adjustments. By bridging onboard IoT hardware with NASA space science, LunaLog delivers a flight-ready logistics guardian that protects astronauts and preserves mission-critical supplies for sustainable Artemis base camps and future human expeditions to Mars.

RoverGuard.AI

RoverGuard.AI is a web-based mission-control and fault-tolerance system designed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It supports autonomous rover operations where communication delays make continuous remote control impractical. From a dashboard hosted at localhost:5000, users can switch between the Artemis South Pole on the Moon and Jezero Crater on Mars while monitoring mission elapsed time and signal delay. Its interactive digital twin presents a 3D rover in isometric, top-down, and side views, alongside a thermal heatmap that marks temperatures below 45°C as nominal, 45–75°C as warning, and above 75°C as critical. Subsystem cards report drive-motor health at 100%, the Li-ion electrical power system (EPS) at 28.4 V and 24°C, vapor levels at 14 PPM, and avionics/IMU vibration at 0.12 G. An autonomous emergency decision engine assesses whether the rover is safe, identifies likely failing components, estimates severity and remaining useful life (RUL), and recommends an action with an explanation. The multi-zone temperature engine tracks motor, battery, and avionics temperatures—including a motor reading of 34.6°C—plots temperature trends against the 75°C runaway ceiling, and displays a 40.4°C thermal margin. The GPS/XY localization and waypoint radar reports an RTK-orbital fix, HDOP of 0.82, and coordinates of X +148.6 m and Y −82.2 m; an autonomous route planner can avoid hazards such as crater rims and steep regolith slopes, including an 8.2° grade. A sensor reliability matrix applies gradient, velocity, and rate-of-rise checks to distinguish sensor faults from rover faults. For live demonstrations, the fault injection studio provides six scenarios, including motor overheating, GPS drift, sensor glitches, regolith hazards, and VOC outgassing, using an ESP32/RP2040 hardware stack.
